summary: Sets out requirements for an Internet audio codec, covering quality, sampling rate, bit rate, and robustness to packet loss, as well as other useful properties. It is informational and fed into later codec work.

eli5.summary: Before inventing a new way to squeeze sound for the internet, you list what it should do well. This is that list: good sound, small size, and still works when pieces get lost.

questions: requirements for a wideband audio codec
what are the requirements for an internet audio codec
what packet loss must an internet audio codec tolerate
what sampling rates are narrowband and wideband
subtitle: The checklist an audio codec has to meet to work well for calls, conferences, games and music over the Internet.

tldr.problem: Interactive audio on the Internet faces packet loss, varying bandwidth and strict delay limits, and no agreed list existed of what a codec built for it must achieve.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC surveys target applications and Internet constraints, then sets requirements for operating space, quality versus bit-rate, packet-loss robustness and computational resources, plus optional extras.
tldr.outcome: It is an Informational requirements document. It sets targets and comparison codecs but does not define a codec itself.

facts.label: Loss tolerance
facts.value: acceptable quality up to 5%, intelligible up to 15%

today: RFC 6366 is an Informational document, published in August 2011. The unit metadata shows no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: Purpose and Definitions
sections.content:
This document gives requirements for an audio codec designed specifically for use over the Internet. It addresses quality, sampling rate, delay, bit-rate and packet-loss robustness, and considers other desirable properties.

It uses four labels for sampling rate: narrowband is 8 kHz, wideband 16 kHz, super-wideband 24/32 kHz and full-band 44.1/48 kHz. Bit-rates are counted without IP/UDP/RTP headers or padding. Codec delay is the algorithmic delay: the frame size plus look-ahead, the minimum theoretically achievable end-to-end delay.
sections.eli5: This is a wish list for a way of shrinking sound so it travels well over the Internet. It also names the sound qualities, from phone-like to full music quality.

sections.title: Target Applications
sections.content:
The RFC lists applications and what each needs. Point-to-point calls need a wideband codec with narrowband support for compatibility with the PSTN, at 12 - 32 kbit/s for wideband and 8 - 16 kbit/s for narrowband, with codec delay under 40 ms (25 ms desirable). Conferencing needs super-wideband at 32 - 64 kbit/s, delay under 30 ms, and cheap mixing, including estimating voice activity without fully decoding a packet.

Telepresence adds super-wideband and full-band at 32 - 80 kbit/s and multi-channel support. Teleoperation and remote software services need delay below 10 ms. In-game voice chat resembles conferencing without the narrowband need and values a low-delay option and variable bit-rate. Live music needs the lowest delay: musicians tolerate end-to-end delay up to 25 ms with about 50 ms as the absolute limit, leaving around 2 ms to 10 ms for the codec, at roughly 64 kbit/s to 128 kbit/s per channel. Delay-tolerant and push-to-talk uses need playout that can pause for an arbitrary time.
sections.eli5: Phone calls, group meetings, video games and bands playing together over the Internet all need different things. Bands need the least waiting, and meetings need the sound easy to mix.

sections.title: Constraints from the Internet
sections.content:
Packet loss is inevitable, so it should be possible to interpret any received packet regardless of earlier losses, and the decoder should resynchronize quickly. A compressed frame must be smaller than the MTU to avoid fragmentation, and no parameter may depend on information in other packets. Some prediction across frames is fine if it recovers quickly, ideally with real-time control of the trade-off between efficiency and robustness.

The Internet is mostly best-effort with no guaranteed bandwidth, so the codec has to vary its bit-rate in real time without out-of-band signaling or audible artifacts. A codec should produce whole bytes, may consider explicit congestion notification (ECN), and must allow an RTP payload format that conforms to BCP 36. Any negotiation should be easy over SIP/SDP or XMPP/Jingle. Decoder-only error concealment does not need specifying, though a working concealment algorithm is desirable in the reference implementation.
sections.eli5: Internet packets sometimes get lost, and the speed changes all the time. So each piece of sound must make sense by itself, and the codec must be able to speed up or slow down smoothly.

sections.title: Detailed Basic Requirements
sections.content:
Applications split into medium delay (20-30 ms) and very low delay (under 10 ms). For medium delay, per-channel bit-rates must be efficient across narrowband 8 to 16 kbit/s, wideband 12 to 32, super-wideband 24 to 64 and full-band 32 to 80 kbit/s. For very low delay: super-wideband 32 to 80 and full-band 48 to 128 kbit/s.

On quality, the codec must beat generally royalty-free codecs: Speex and iLBC for narrowband, Speex and G.722.1 for wideband, and G.722.1C for super-wideband and full-band. It should be no worse than AMR-NB and AMR-WB. Quality must be tested on multiple languages, including tonal ones. Source-controlled VBR is desirable, but truly constant bit-rate must remain possible.

For loss, codecs must keep acceptable quality at loss rates up to 5% and good intelligibility up to 15%, never worse than Speex or GSM-FR, using real loss traces. Computational limits for mono on one x86 core: narrowband 40 MHz, wideband 80 MHz, super-wideband and full-band 200 MHz. State size should be no more than 2*R*C bytes in floating-point and under R*C for fixed-point.
sections.eli5: The list gives the sizes the sound can use and says the new codec must sound better than older free ones. It must keep working when some pieces go missing and run on small, cheap devices.

sections.title: Additional Considerations
sections.content:
A set of nice-to-haves should be weighed against their cost. They are low-complexity mixing, room to improve the encoder without changing the decoder, a layered bit-stream, partial redundancy that can be switched on and off, stereo support, extra bit error robustness (but never at the expense of packet-loss robustness), time stretching and shortening for adaptive jitter buffers, graceful behavior with poor input, and support for audio forensics.

For forensics, the encoder must allow DTX to be disabled, for example for emergency calls, so background sound is kept. The RFC states there is no requirement for compatibility with legacy Internet codecs.
sections.eli5: Extra wishes include easy mixing of many voices and keeping background noise for emergency calls. None of them are strict rules.

sections.title: Security Requirements for the Codec
sections.content:
The document itself has no security considerations, but it states security requirements for the codec. Decoders must have a bounded and reasonable worst-case complexity, so crafted packets cannot cause a denial of service by taking very long to decode.

Over an encrypted channel such as SRTP, source-controlled VBR may reveal information about a conversation through packet sizes. So it should be possible to use the codec at a truly constant bit-rate if needed.
sections.eli5: A codec should never be made to freeze by a trick packet. And if the size of packets changes with what is said, a snooper could guess things, so there should be a fixed-size setting.
